flawed_step: Step 2: inferring vertex-transitivity from regularity and edge-transitivity is unjustified. Edge-transitivity can leave the two endpoint classes of a bipartite graph as distinct vertex orbits; regularity only forces those classes to have equal size, not an automorphism interchanging them.
counterexample: Let P=Z_3^3. Let L consist of the 27 axis-parallel lines in Z_3^3: for each coordinate direction i and each choice of values for the other two coordinates, include one line. Form the bipartite incidence graph G with vertex set P disjoint union L, joining a point to each axis-parallel line containing it. This is a finite simple graph with 54 vertices. Every point lies on exactly three lines, and every line contains exactly three points, so G is 3-regular. It is edge-transitive: coordinate permutations and independent permutations of the three values in each coordinate preserve incidence and can send any incident point-line pair to any other. It is not vertex-transitive. For p=(0,0,0), the numbers of vertices at distances 0 through 6 are (1,3,6,12,12,12,8). For the line ell={(x,0,0):x in Z_3}, they are (1,3,6,12,16,12,4). Specifically, from ell the 16 vertices at distance 4 are the four parallel lines differing in exactly one fixed coordinate and the twelve nonintersecting perpendicular lines. Since automorphisms preserve graph distances and distance-sphere sizes, no automorphism sends p to ell. Thus G is regular and edge-transitive but not vertex-transitive.
assessment_summary: 1. Edge-transitivity does imply that all edges are structurally equivalent. 2. It does not imply that the two endpoints of an edge lie in one vertex orbit; they may form two invariant bipartition classes. 3. Regularity does not eliminate that possibility. The explicit 54-vertex incidence graph above realizes it, so the universal statement is false.
